title: NCLEX: Pharmacology Drug Classes
description: For nursing students reviewing 50 drug classes: generic examples, mechanisms, major adverse effects and nursing priorities. Educational review; verify with current guidelines and product-specific orders.

sources.name: DailyMed prescribing information
sources.license: Publicly accessible drug labeling; original summaries

cards.front: ACE inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: lisinopril, enalapril.

cards.front: ACE inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II and aldosterone and increasing bradykinin.

cards.front: ACE inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Cough, hyperkalemia, hypotension, kidney function changes and potentially life-threatening angioedema.

cards.front: ACE inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor blood pressure, potassium and renal function. Escalate facial or airway swelling immediately. Avoid use during pregnancy.

cards.front: Angiotensin II receptor blockers: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: losartan, valsartan.

cards.front: Angiotensin II receptor blockers: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block angiotensin II at AT1 receptors, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone effects.

cards.front: Angiotensin II receptor blockers: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia, hypotension and kidney function changes; angioedema is possible.

cards.front: Angiotensin II receptor blockers: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor blood pressure, potassium and renal function. Avoid pregnancy and routine combination with an ACE inhibitor.

cards.front: Beta blockers: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: metoprolol, propranolol.

cards.front: Beta blockers: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block beta-adrenergic receptors; cardiac beta-1 blockade lowers heart rate, contractility and renin release.

cards.front: Beta blockers: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bradycardia, hypotension and fatigue; nonselective agents may cause bronchospasm. Some hypoglycemia warning signs may be masked.

cards.front: Beta blockers: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess pulse and blood pressure against ordered parameters. Review asthma and diabetes history. Avoid abrupt discontinuation.

cards.front: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: amlodipine, nifedipine.

cards.front: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block L-type calcium channels mainly in vascular smooth muscle, causing arterial dilation.

cards.front: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Peripheral edema, headache, flushing and hypotension.

cards.front: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor blood pressure, dizziness and edema. Teach gradual position changes and distinguish edema from fluid overload using the full assessment.

cards.front: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: diltiazem, verapamil.

cards.front: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block L-type calcium channels in the heart and vessels; slow AV conduction and reduce contractility.

cards.front: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bradycardia, AV block, hypotension and worsening systolic heart failure; constipation is prominent with verapamil.

cards.front: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess heart rate, blood pressure and ECG when indicated. Review concurrent beta blockers and avoid use in unsuitable conduction disorders.

cards.front: Loop diuretics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: furosemide, bumetanide.

cards.front: Loop diuretics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

cards.front: Loop diuretics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Volume depletion, hypokalemia, hyponatremia and possible ototoxicity.

cards.front: Loop diuretics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor intake/output, daily weight, blood pressure, electrolytes and renal function. Follow prescribed IV administration rates.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit sodium-chloride transport in the distal convoluted tubule.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and dehydration.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor blood pressure, electrolytes and volume status; review gout history and fall risk.

cards.front: Aldosterone antagonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: spironolactone, eplerenone.

cards.front: Aldosterone antagonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block mineralocorticoid receptors, increasing sodium excretion while conserving potassium.

cards.front: Aldosterone antagonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia and renal impairment; spironolactone can cause gynecomastia.

cards.front: Aldosterone antagonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor potassium and renal function. Review potassium supplements, salt substitutes and other potassium-raising drugs.

cards.front: Organic nitrates: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate.

cards.front: Organic nitrates: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Generate nitric oxide signaling that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, especially veins, reducing preload.

cards.front: Organic nitrates: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Headache, hypotension, dizziness and reflex tachycardia.

cards.front: Organic nitrates: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess blood pressure and pain. Check for phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use because combined use can cause severe hypotension. Follow the formulation-specific schedule.

cards.front: Statins: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: atorvastatin, rosuvastatin.

cards.front: Statins: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and increase hepatic LDL receptor activity, lowering LDL cholesterol.

cards.front: Statins: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Muscle symptoms, rare rhabdomyolysis and liver enzyme elevations.

cards.front: Statins: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess unexplained muscle pain or dark urine promptly. Review interactions and liver tests as indicated; discuss pregnancy plans with the prescriber.

cards.front: Cardiac glycosides: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: digoxin.

cards.front: Cardiac glycosides: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit sodium-potassium ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium and contractility; vagal effects slow AV conduction.

cards.front: Cardiac glycosides: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Nausea, visual changes, bradycardia and other dysrhythmias with toxicity.

cards.front: Cardiac glycosides: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor pulse, renal function, potassium and appropriately timed drug levels. Hypokalemia increases toxicity risk.

cards.front: Vitamin K antagonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: warfarin.

cards.front: Vitamin K antagonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Reduce regeneration of active vitamin K, decreasing synthesis of functional factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

cards.front: Vitamin K antagonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bleeding; rare skin necrosis; fetal harm.

cards.front: Vitamin K antagonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor INR and bleeding. Teach consistent vitamin K intake and interaction checks. Effects develop over days rather than immediately.

cards.front: Unfractionated heparins: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: heparin.

cards.front: Unfractionated heparins: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Enhance antithrombin activity against thrombin and factor Xa.

cards.front: Unfractionated heparins: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which may cause thrombosis.

cards.front: Unfractionated heparins: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: For therapeutic infusions, monitor aPTT or anti-Xa per protocol, platelets and bleeding. Protamine can reverse anticoagulant effects when prescribed.

cards.front: Low-molecular-weight heparins: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: enoxaparin, dalteparin.

cards.front: Low-molecular-weight heparins: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Enhance antithrombin activity, with greater inhibition of factor Xa than thrombin.

cards.front: Low-molecular-weight heparins: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bleeding and possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

cards.front: Low-molecular-weight heparins: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Review renal function, weight and platelet history. Routine aPTT does not measure their effect; anti-Xa monitoring is reserved for selected situations.

cards.front: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: apixaban, rivaroxaban.

cards.front: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Directly inhibit factor Xa and reduce thrombin generation.

cards.front: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bleeding, including serious internal bleeding.

cards.front: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor bleeding, renal/hepatic function and interactions. Routine INR is not used to adjust dosing; missed doses can reduce protection quickly.

cards.front: P2Y12 platelet inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: clopidogrel, prasugrel.

cards.front: P2Y12 platelet inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block platelet ADP P2Y12 receptors, reducing platelet activation and aggregation.

cards.front: P2Y12 platelet inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bleeding and bruising; rare thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

cards.front: P2Y12 platelet inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor bleeding and planned procedures. Do not independently stop therapy after coronary stenting; premature interruption can cause thrombosis.

cards.front: Fibrinolytics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: alteplase, tenecteplase.

cards.front: Fibrinolytics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Promote conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin in thrombi.

cards.front: Fibrinolytics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Major bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage.

cards.front: Fibrinolytics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Confirm indication-specific eligibility and contraindications; monitor neurologic status, blood pressure and bleeding closely. Minimize unnecessary invasive procedures.

cards.front: Rapid-acting insulins: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: insulin lispro, insulin aspart.

cards.front: Rapid-acting insulins: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Activate insulin receptors, increasing cellular glucose uptake and lowering hepatic glucose output.

cards.front: Rapid-acting insulins: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hypoglycemia, hypokalemia and injection-site lipodystrophy.

cards.front: Rapid-acting insulins: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Coordinate administration with the product-specific meal plan. Check glucose, ensure food availability and rotate injection sites.

cards.front: Long-acting basal insulins: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: insulin glargine, insulin degludec.

cards.front: Long-acting basal insulins: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Provide prolonged insulin receptor stimulation to cover basal glucose needs.

cards.front: Long-acting basal insulins: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hypoglycemia, hypokalemia and weight gain.

cards.front: Long-acting basal insulins: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Verify product and concentration, monitor glucose and follow scheduled dosing. Do not mix glargine or degludec with other insulins.

cards.front: Biguanides: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: metformin.

cards.front: Biguanides: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Primarily reduce hepatic glucose production and improve insulin sensitivity.

cards.front: Biguanides: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Gastrointestinal upset, vitamin B12 deficiency with long use and rare lactic acidosis.

cards.front: Biguanides: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess renal function; contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Take with meals and follow current instructions for acute illness or iodinated contrast.

cards.front: Sulfonylureas: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: glipizide, glimepiride.

cards.front: Sulfonylureas: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Close ATP-sensitive potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells, stimulating insulin release.

cards.front: Sulfonylureas: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hypoglycemia and weight gain.

cards.front: Sulfonylureas: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Coordinate doses with meals and monitor glucose. Teach hypoglycemia recognition; risk increases with missed meals and impaired drug clearance.

cards.front: SGLT2 inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin.

cards.front: SGLT2 inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Reduce proximal renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose excretion.

cards.front: SGLT2 inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Genital fungal infections, volume depletion and ketoacidosis that may occur without marked hyperglycemia.

cards.front: SGLT2 inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor volume and renal status. Teach prompt reporting of ketoacidosis symptoms and follow current perioperative and sick-day withholding instructions.

cards.front: GLP-1 receptor agonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: semaglutide, liraglutide.

cards.front: GLP-1 receptor agonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduce glucagon, delay gastric emptying and promote satiety.

cards.front: GLP-1 receptor agonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Nausea, vomiting and gallbladder problems; pancreatitis is a serious concern.

cards.front: GLP-1 receptor agonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach product-specific administration, hydration and reporting of persistent severe abdominal pain. Review contraindications, including medullary thyroid cancer history for these agents.

cards.front: Systemic glucocorticoids: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: prednisone, dexamethasone.

cards.front: Systemic glucocorticoids: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Activate intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, changing gene transcription to suppress inflammation and immune responses.

cards.front: Systemic glucocorticoids: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hyperglycemia, infection risk, mood changes, osteoporosis and adrenal suppression with sustained exposure.

cards.front: Systemic glucocorticoids: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor glucose and infection. Do not abruptly stop prolonged therapy; taper only as ordered. Review bone protection for long-term use.

cards.front: Thyroid hormone replacement: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: levothyroxine.

cards.front: Thyroid hormone replacement: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Supplies T4, which is converted to active T3 to support thyroid hormone effects.

cards.front: Thyroid hormone replacement: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Excess replacement can cause tachycardia, heat intolerance, insomnia and bone loss.

cards.front: Thyroid hormone replacement: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Administer consistently, usually on an empty stomach. Separate calcium and iron by the recommended interval; monitor TSH as ordered.

cards.front: Thionamides: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: methimazole, propylthiouracil.

cards.front: Thionamides: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit thyroid peroxidase and thyroid hormone synthesis; propylthiouracil also reduces peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

cards.front: Thionamides: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Agranulocytosis and liver injury; propylthiouracil carries particular concern for severe hepatotoxicity.

cards.front: Thionamides: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach urgent reporting of fever or sore throat and signs of liver injury. Monitor thyroid tests and follow drug-specific pregnancy guidance.

cards.front: Bisphosphonates: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: alendronate, risedronate.

cards.front: Bisphosphonates: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

cards.front: Bisphosphonates: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Oral esophageal irritation, hypocalcemia and rare jaw osteonecrosis or atypical femoral fracture.

cards.front: Bisphosphonates: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: For immediate-release alendronate, take with plain water before food and remain upright at least 30 minutes and until after eating. Review calcium status and dental concerns.

cards.front: Short-acting beta-2 agonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: albuterol, levalbuterol.

cards.front: Short-acting beta-2 agonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Stimulate beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle, producing bronchodilation.

cards.front: Short-acting beta-2 agonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Tremor, tachycardia and hypokalemia, especially with high exposure.

cards.front: Short-acting beta-2 agonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess breath sounds and respiratory response. Teach inhaler technique and report increasing rescue use as a sign of poor control.

cards.front: Inhaled corticosteroids: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: budesonide, fluticasone.

cards.front: Inhaled corticosteroids: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Suppress airway inflammation through glucocorticoid receptor effects.

cards.front: Inhaled corticosteroids: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Oral candidiasis and dysphonia; systemic effects can occur with higher exposure.

cards.front: Inhaled corticosteroids: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach regular use and mouth rinsing after doses. These drugs alone do not provide immediate rescue bronchodilation.

cards.front: Inhaled antimuscarinics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: ipratropium, tiotropium.

cards.front: Inhaled antimuscarinics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block muscarinic receptors in airways, reducing cholinergic bronchoconstriction.

cards.front: Inhaled antimuscarinics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Dry mouth; urinary retention and eye complications can occur in susceptible patients.

cards.front: Inhaled antimuscarinics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach device technique, avoid spraying into eyes and review urinary retention or glaucoma history. Rescue versus maintenance use depends on the product.

cards.front: First-generation H1 antihistamines: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine.

cards.front: First-generation H1 antihistamines: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block histamine H1 effects and also have antimuscarinic activity.

cards.front: First-generation H1 antihistamines: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Sedation, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and confusion.

cards.front: First-generation H1 antihistamines: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess fall risk and anticholinergic burden, especially in older adults. Avoid alcohol and hazardous tasks when sedated.

cards.front: Proton pump inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: omeprazole, pantoprazole.

cards.front: Proton pump inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit the gastric parietal-cell hydrogen-potassium ATPase, strongly reducing acid secretion.

cards.front: Proton pump inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Headache and diarrhea; longer exposure is associated with hypomagnesemia and certain enteric infections.

cards.front: Proton pump inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Follow formulation instructions, commonly dosing before meals. Review ongoing indication and evaluate persistent diarrhea or suspected electrolyte abnormalities.

cards.front: H2 receptor antagonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: famotidine, cimetidine.

cards.front: H2 receptor antagonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion.

cards.front: H2 receptor antagonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Headache and possible confusion, especially with impaired clearance; cimetidine has many interactions.

cards.front: H2 receptor antagonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Review renal function and prescribed dose adjustment. Check interactions, particularly with cimetidine.

cards.front: Osmotic laxatives: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: polyethylene glycol, lactulose.

cards.front: Osmotic laxatives: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Retain water in the bowel to soften stool and promote evacuation.

cards.front: Osmotic laxatives: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Bloating, cramps, diarrhea and fluid or electrolyte imbalance with excessive effect.

cards.front: Osmotic laxatives: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess bowel pattern, hydration and possible obstruction before use. For lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy, follow the ordered stool goal.

cards.front: Stimulant laxatives: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: senna, bisacodyl.

cards.front: Stimulant laxatives: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Stimulate intestinal motility and secretion.

cards.front: Stimulant laxatives: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Abdominal cramping, diarrhea and electrolyte losses.

cards.front: Stimulant laxatives: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess unexplained severe abdominal pain before administration; monitor bowel response and avoid unprescribed overuse.

cards.front: 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: ondansetron, granisetron.

cards.front: 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in emetic pathways.

cards.front: 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Headache, constipation and QT prolongation.

cards.front: 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Review QT-risk drugs and electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor ECG when indicated and assess response to nausea treatment.

cards.front: Opioid agonist analgesics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: morphine, fentanyl.

cards.front: Opioid agonist analgesics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Activate opioid receptors, especially mu receptors, reducing pain transmission and perception.

cards.front: Opioid agonist analgesics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea and dependence.

cards.front: Opioid agonist analgesics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor sedation and ventilation, not pain score alone. Review other sedatives, implement bowel care and maintain access to naloxone per protocol.

cards.front: Opioid antagonists: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: naloxone, naltrexone.

cards.front: Opioid antagonists: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Block opioid receptors and prevent or reverse opioid effects.

cards.front: Opioid antagonists: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Precipitated withdrawal; pain can return after reversal.

cards.front: Opioid antagonists: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: For naloxone rescue, support breathing and watch for recurrent respiratory depression because its action may be shorter than the opioid's. Repeat treatment per protocol.

cards.front: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: ibuprofen, naproxen.

cards.front: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes and reduce prostaglandin synthesis.

cards.front: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention and cardiovascular risk.

cards.front: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Review renal function, bleeding history and concurrent anticoagulants. Avoid duplicate NSAIDs and follow pregnancy-specific restrictions.

cards.front: Benzodiazepines: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: lorazepam, diazepam.

cards.front: Benzodiazepines: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Enhance GABA-A receptor responses, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening in the presence of GABA.

cards.front: Benzodiazepines: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Sedation, falls, dependence and respiratory depression, especially with other depressants.

cards.front: Benzodiazepines: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor alertness and respiration. Avoid alcohol and concurrent sedatives unless specifically managed; taper sustained use as ordered to prevent withdrawal.

cards.front: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: sertraline, fluoxetine.

cards.front: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonergic signaling.

cards.front: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Gastrointestinal upset, sexual dysfunction, hyponatremia, bleeding tendency and serotonin syndrome risk.

cards.front: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor mood and suicidality, especially early or after dose changes. Explain delayed benefit and review serotonergic interactions.

cards.front: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: venlafaxine, duloxetine.

cards.front: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.

cards.front: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Nausea, sexual dysfunction, blood pressure elevation and discontinuation symptoms.

cards.front: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor blood pressure and mood. Taper as ordered and check serotonergic interactions; avoid abrupt cessation.

cards.front: Tricyclic antidepressants: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: amitriptyline, nortriptyline.

cards.front: Tricyclic antidepressants: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and also block several other receptors.

cards.front: Tricyclic antidepressants: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension and dangerous cardiac toxicity in overdose.

cards.front: Tricyclic antidepressants: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess falls, cardiac history and suicide risk. Monitor ECG when indicated and reinforce prescribed dosing and secure storage.

cards.front: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: phenelzine, tranylcypromine.

cards.front: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Inhibit monoamine oxidase, increasing monoamine availability.

cards.front: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Orthostatic hypotension, serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crisis with tyramine or interacting drugs.

cards.front: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach tyramine restrictions and medication checks. Observe drug-specific washout intervals when changing interacting antidepressants.

cards.front: First-generation antipsychotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: haloperidol, chlorpromazine.

cards.front: First-generation antipsychotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Primarily block dopamine D2 receptors.

cards.front: First-generation antipsychotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

cards.front: First-generation antipsychotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Assess movement symptoms and mental status. Fever with rigidity and autonomic instability requires urgent evaluation; monitor QT risk when indicated.

cards.front: Second-generation antipsychotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: risperidone, olanzapine.

cards.front: Second-generation antipsychotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Typically antagonize dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors; effects vary by agent.

cards.front: Second-generation antipsychotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Weight gain, dyslipidemia and hyperglycemia; movement effects and neuroleptic malignant syndrome remain possible.

cards.front: Second-generation antipsychotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor weight, glucose, lipids and movement symptoms. Review orthostasis and agent-specific monitoring requirements.

cards.front: Penicillin antibiotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: penicillin G, amoxicillin.

cards.front: Penicillin antibiotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit bacterial cell-wall cross-linking.

cards.front: Penicillin antibiotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and diarrhea including possible C. difficile infection.

cards.front: Penicillin antibiotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Clarify allergy reaction history, obtain ordered cultures before therapy when feasible and monitor response and serious diarrhea.

cards.front: Cephalosporin antibiotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: cephalexin, ceftriaxone.

cards.front: Cephalosporin antibiotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis.

cards.front: Cephalosporin antibiotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Hypersensitivity and diarrhea including possible C. difficile infection.

cards.front: Cephalosporin antibiotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Review severe beta-lactam allergy history and drug-specific renal or biliary considerations. Monitor infection response and infusion site as appropriate.

cards.front: Aminoglycoside antibiotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: gentamicin, tobramycin.

cards.front: Aminoglycoside antibiotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Bind bacterial 30S ribosomes, disrupting protein synthesis and causing misreading of mRNA.

cards.front: Aminoglycoside antibiotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and possible neuromuscular blockade.

cards.front: Aminoglycoside antibiotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Monitor renal function and drug levels according to the dosing strategy. Assess hearing or balance changes and review other nephrotoxic drugs.

cards.front: Tetracycline antibiotics: name representative generic drugs.
cards.back: doxycycline, tetracycline.

cards.front: Tetracycline antibiotics: what is the main mechanism?
cards.back: Bind bacterial 30S ribosomes and impede attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA.

cards.front: Tetracycline antibiotics: what key adverse effects should be recognized?
cards.back: Photosensitivity, gastrointestinal upset and esophageal irritation; effects on developing teeth are agent- and context-dependent.

cards.front: Tetracycline antibiotics: what are priority nursing considerations?
cards.back: Teach sun protection and separation from polyvalent cations per product guidance. Take oral doxycycline with water and avoid lying down immediately; follow age- and pregnancy-specific prescribing guidance.
